statement_pretty:
∀ {α : Type} [inst_2 : LE α] (S : Set (UpperSet α)) {u : Set α},
  ⋃ s ∈ S, ↑s ⊆ u →
    ∀ {v w : Set α}, v \ u ⊂ w → Set.Ioc ((v \ ↑(sInf S)) \ (u \ ↑(sInf S))) w ≠ ∅

referees.justification: Calibrated zero-token rubric evaluation assigns an expected importance of 3.52/10 (confidence 0.29) and classifies the result as a Lemma (p = 0.49) in MSC 06-XX. Independent probability estimates yield P(surprising) = 0.43 and P(a human mathematician cares) = 0.20.

This result is an elementary set-theoretic observation disguised by an artificial invocation of upper sets and half-open intervals in the power set lattice. While formally sound, the hypotheses are needlessly convoluted and the conclusion follows from routine manipulations of set differences, warranting classification as a minor lemma of negligible mathematical significance.

editorial.title: The Upper-Set Infimum-Difference Interval Lemma

editorial.unverified_gloss:
For a type α with a ≤ relation, a family S of upper sets in α, and subsets u, v, w ⊆ α, if u contains the union of all sets in S and v \ u is a strict subset of w, then the half-open interval (a, w] in the subset-inclusion order on Set α is nonempty, where a = (v \ ↑(sInf S)) \ (u \ ↑(sInf S)).

The hypothesis ⋃ s ∈ S, ↑s ⊆ u ensures that ↑(sInf S) ⊆ u, which makes the complicated set-difference expression a collapse to v \ u. Because v \ u ⊂ w, the set w itself belongs to the interval (v \ u, w], so the nonemptiness conclusion is an immediate consequence of rewriting a and observing that w is the greatest element of (a, w].
